claims.claim: Performance management is the ongoing process of setting expectations, measuring results, and developing people; OPM defines it as the systematic process by which an agency involves its employees in improving organizational effectiveness in the accomplishment of mission and goals.

Investopedia defines performance management as a tool that helps managers monitor and evaluate employees' work, with the goal of creating an environment where people can perform to the best of their abilities in alignment with the organization's overall goals.

Performance management is a continuous cycle; OPM's version has five components: planning (setting expectations and goals in advance), monitoring progress continually, developing ability through training and work assignments, rating periodically to summarize performance, and rewarding good performance.

A performance appraisal is a comparison of actual performance with expected performance, used to make decisions about training, compensation, promotion, and other job changes; a performance improvement plan outlines the behaviors to improve, the milestones and time periods, and what happens if performance does not improve.
Most companies have moved away from annual-only appraisals and encourage continuous, real-time feedback so skill development and job performance improve more rapidly.

Performance management originated with the U.S. military's merit-rating system created during World War I to identify poor performers; after World War II about 60% of U.S. companies used performance appraisal, and by the 1960s nearly 90% did.

Effective performance management programs align employees' activities with company mission and goals, define job outcomes, create measurable performance-based expectations with employee input, define job-development plans, and meet regularly year-round rather than only at the annual appraisal.

Good feedback is regular and specific, and Gallup frames effective performance management as managers acting as coaches rather than bosses; ongoing feedback means employees face fewer unpleasant surprises at the year-end review.

Documented pitfalls of performance reviews include: annual-only reviews letting problems fester because managers overlook poor performance during the year and address it ineffectively at the single review; subjective ratings and ratings bias; and forced ranking, which GE abandoned after it fostered internal competition and undermined collaboration.

A Deloitte survey found that 58% of executives believed their current performance management approach drives neither employee engagement nor high performance, spurring redesigns toward more frequent feedback.

Development is a core step of the cycle: OPM's developing component uses training and work assignments, Investopedia lists job-development plans as a universal program element, and performance management has evolved from an accountability tool into a development tool.

Fairness matters: a CEB survey of more than 9,000 managers and employees found that employees accept unfavorable outcomes more readily when the process is fair, and real-time communication and documentation is the best strategy for effective and fair performance management.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How often formal performance evaluation should occur: continuous-feedback redesigns versus the annual review.
positions: Continuous real-time feedback should replace or dominate the annual review (OpenStax Introduction to Business notes most companies moved away from annual-only appraisals; OpenStax Principles of Management reports some companies discussed dropping formal appraisals entirely)
The formal evaluation must remain: a CEB survey of more than 9,000 managers and employees found that not having performance evaluations is worse than having them (OpenStax Principles of Management)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both: the formal review stays a step in the cycle, but it only works as a summary of ongoing, real-time feedback. The review is kept; the annual-only habit is dropped.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Forced ranking (grading employees against one another) as a performance management tool.
positions: Early advocates such as GE under Jack Welch used forced ranking to differentiate performance and shed poor performers
Critics — and later GE itself — dropped it, finding it fostered internal competition and undermined collaboration and teamwork
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the practice factually and treats it as a documented pitfall rather than a recommendation.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Business, Section 8.5: Performance Planning and Evaluation
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Record reused from the phase-2 source registry (identical id and URL); content re-verified live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Supports: performance appraisal as a comparison of actual performance with expected performance used to make decisions about training, compensation, promotion, and other job changes; the manager establishing standards, the employee working to meet them, and reward/job-change decisions following evaluation; performance improvement plans (behaviors to improve, milestones and time periods, consequences); rewards as positive feedback and reinforcement; the shift from annual appraisals toward continuous real-time feedback; sources of appraisal information (rating scales, supervisor logs, sales and production statistics). Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Management, Section 11.3: Performance Management
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Verified live via HTTP on 2026-08-22 (server-rendered page). Supports: origins of performance management in the U.S. military's merit-rating system (World War I) and its evolution from an accountability tool into a development tool; ~60% of U.S. companies using appraisal after World War II and nearly 90% by the 1960s; GE's forced ranking under Jack Welch (1981) and GE's later abandonment of it for undermining collaboration and teamwork; a Deloitte survey finding 58% of executives said their approach drives neither engagement nor high performance; a CEB survey of more than 9,000 managers and employees finding that not having evaluations is worse than having them and that fair process helps employees accept unfavorable outcomes; challenges of aligning individual and company goals, rewarding performance, and identifying poor performers; annual processes letting problems fester until a one-per-year review; real-time communication and documentation as the best strategy for effective and fair performance management. Facts restated in original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Performance Management Cycle (OPM)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (U.S. federal government; public domain work in the U.S., though the lesson uses it reference-only). Verified live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Supports: OPM's definition of performance management as the systematic process by which an agency involves its employees, as individuals and members of a group, in improving organizational effectiveness in the accomplishment of agency mission and goals; performance management as a continuous cycle with five components — planning (setting performance expectations and goals in advance, including how they will be measured), monitoring progress and performance continually, developing the employee's ability to perform through training and work assignments, rating periodically to summarize performance, and rewarding good performance with formal and informal rewards; the statement that performance management involves much more than assigning ratings. Facts restated in original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Performance Management: Definition, Purpose, Steps & Benefits
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (reputable reference). The live site returns HTTP 403 to automated fetchers, so the page was read via an Internet Archive capture (2024-01-18) of the canonical URL. Supports: performance management as a tool that helps managers monitor and evaluate employees' work so people can perform to the best of their abilities in alignment with the organization's goals; universal program elements — aligning employees' activities with the company's mission and goals, defining job outcomes, creating measurable performance-based expectations with employee input, defining job-development plans, and meeting regularly year-round instead of waiting for the annual appraisal; ongoing feedback reducing year-end surprises; Gallup's framing that effective performance management requires managers to think of themselves as coaches, not bosses; the distinction between performance management and performance appraisal. Facts restated in original prose; no wording reproduced.
